--- title: "Skill-Gap Analysis" subtitle: "Team Skills Compared With Analytics Job Postings in NAICS 5415" bibliography: references.bib csl: csl/econometrica.csl toc: true execute: echo: true warning: false format: html: code-fold: true code-summary: "Show code" --- ## Purpose This page compares the skills requested in our analytics job postings with the current skills of our three team members. It answers two supporting questions from the Project Overview: - Where does the target user have skill gaps? - Which skills should the target user prioritize? We use our own team as three realistic examples of the target user: early-career candidates moving into analytics roles within Computer Systems Design and Related Services (NAICS 5415). ::: {.callout-note} ## Data Source This analysis uses the corrected v2 extract described on the [Data Preparation](data_cleaning.qmd) page: 1,790 analytics postings posted between September 2025 and September 2026. Unlike the original extract, v2 contains the full skill taxonomy, so core tools such as Python, SQL, Tableau, and Power BI are measured directly in the postings. ::: ## 1. Team Skill Ratings Each team member rated their current proficiency on the course's five-point scale: | Score | Level | |:---:|---| | 1 | Beginner | | 2 | Basic knowledge | | 3 | Intermediate | | 4 | Advanced | | 5 | Expert | The skill list comes from the postings themselves: it covers the most requested tools and competencies that a person can realistically rate and learn. Very broad fields such as "Data Science" or "Computer Science" were left out because they describe a discipline rather than a skill. | Team member | Target role | Background | |---|---|---| | Jenna | Business Intelligence / Business Analyst | Strong Excel, BI, and communication skills; some Power BI; beginner in coding | | Mariam | Business Analyst | Strong business requirements and analysis skills; beginner in coding | | Juan | Data Analyst, moving toward Data Scientist | Expert in Excel, Power BI, Tableau, and data analysis; intermediate in SQL and Python | The ratings are stored in `data/processed/team_skills_v2.csv`. This page and the Improvement Plan below both read from that one file, so updating a rating there updates the whole analysis. ::: {#tbl-team-skills .cell tbl-cap='Self-assessed skill levels (1 = Beginner, 5 = Expert).' execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} MEMBERS = ["Jenna", "Mariam", "Juan"] ratings = pd.read_csv("data/processed/team_skills_v2.csv").set_index("skill") # Team skill dataframe: one row per member, one column per skill df_skills = ratings[MEMBERS].T df_skills.index.name = "Name" df_skills.T.rename_axis("Skill").rename_axis(None, axis=1).reset_index().style.hide(axis="index") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Team Skill Heatmap ::: {#cell-fig-team-heatmap .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} heat = df_skills.T.loc[df_skills.mean().sort_values(ascending=False).index] fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 7.5)) annotated_heatmap(ax, heat, SEQUENTIAL, vmin=1, vmax=5, fmt=lambda v: f"{v:.0f}", dark_from=3) ax.set_title("Team Skill Levels (1 = Beginner, 5 = Expert)", pad=28) save_figure("team_skill_heatmap.png") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Team skill levels, sorted by team average. Darker cells show stronger skills.](skill_gap_analysis_files/figure-html/fig-team-heatmap-output-1.png){#fig-team-heatmap width=621 height=711} ::: ::: The heatmap shows a clear split between business and technical skills: - **All three members are strong on the business side:** data analysis, business analysis, business requirements, and communication. - **Juan is the team's strongest member overall**, at Expert level in the BI tools (Tableau, Power BI, Excel) and intermediate in SQL and Python. - **Jenna** brings Advanced Excel, business analysis, and communication skills, with intermediate BI tools and data modeling. - **Mariam** is strongest in business requirements, with most technical tools still at Beginner level. The bottom of the heatmap is the shared weak spot. **No one on the team is above Intermediate in Python, SQL, data pipelines, Databricks, machine learning, or statistical modeling.** ## 2. Skills Requested in Job Postings We extracted skills from the `SKILLS_NAME` field. Each posting stores its skills as a list, so we count **how many postings mention each skill** rather than total mentions. This stops a single long posting from inflating a skill's importance. Content analysis of analytics job advertisements has used the same posting-level approach to compare skill requirements across business analyst, data analyst, and data scientist roles [@verma2019skills]. ::: {#extract-skills .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} panel = pd.read_csv("data/processed/career_market_panel.csv") panel["skills"] = panel["SKILLS_NAME"].fillna("[]").map( lambda s: set(json.loads(s)) if s.startswith("[") else set() ) n_postings = len(panel) skill_postings = panel["skills"].explode().dropna().value_counts() print(f"Postings analyzed: {n_postings:,}") print(f"Postings with at least one skill: {(panel['skills'].map(len) > 0).sum():,}") print(f"Distinct skills: {skill_postings.size:,}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Postings analyzed: 1,790 Postings with at least one skill: 1,785 Distinct skills: 1,394 ``` ::: ::: ### Most Requested Skills ::: {#cell-fig-top-skills .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} top = (skill_postings.head(20) / n_postings * 100).sort_values() rated = set(ratings["panel_skill_name"]) colors = [TEAL if skill in rated else LIGHT_BLUE for skill in top.index] fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 7)) bars = ax.barh(top.index, top.values, color=colors, height=0.7) for bar, value in zip(bars, top.values): ax.text(value + 0.8, bar.get_y() + bar.get_height() / 2, f"{value:.0f}%", va="center", fontsize=9, color=NAVY) ax.set_xlabel("Share of postings (%)") ax.set_xlim(0, top.max() * 1.12) ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False) ax.legend( handles=[plt.Rectangle((0, 0), 1, 1, color=TEAL), plt.Rectangle((0, 0), 1, 1, color=LIGHT_BLUE)], labels=["Rated by the team", "Not on the team's list"], loc="lower right", frameon=False, ) ax.set_title("Most Requested Skills in Analytics Postings (NAICS 5415)") save_figure("top_posting_skills.png") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![The 20 skills mentioned in the most postings. Teal bars are skills the team rated; light bars are broad fields or tools outside the team's list.](skill_gap_analysis_files/figure-html/fig-top-skills-output-1.png){#fig-top-skills width=844 height=662} ::: ::: **Python and SQL dominate**, each appearing in more than 60% of postings, roughly three times as often as the next skill. After them comes a mix of data-engineering skills (data pipelines, data engineering, Databricks), data science (machine learning), and BI tools (Tableau, Power BI). Business-side skills such as business requirements and Excel appear in about 10% of postings. ### Demand for the Team's Skills ::: {#tbl-skill-demand .cell tbl-cap='Share of all 1,790 postings that request each skill on the team\'s list.' execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} demand = ratings["panel_skill_name"].map(lambda name: skill_postings.get(name, 0)).rename("Postings") demand = demand.to_frame() demand["Share of postings (%)"] = (demand["Postings"] / n_postings * 100).round(1) demand = demand.sort_values("Postings", ascending=False) demand.rename_axis("Skill").reset_index().style.hide(axis="index").format(precision=1).format("{:,}", subset=["Postings"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ### Demand Depends on the Role The market average hides large differences between roles. The v2 data classifies each posting into a role family, so we can see what each of our target roles asks for. ::: {#cell-fig-role-demand .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} ROLES = ["Business Analyst", "Business Intelligence", "Data Analyst", "Data Scientist", "Data Engineer"] role_demand = pd.DataFrame( { role: ratings["panel_skill_name"].map( lambda name, role=role: panel.loc[panel["role_family"] == role, "skills"] .map(lambda s: name in s).mean() * 100 ) for role in ROLES } ).loc[demand.index] role_counts = panel["role_family"].value_counts() plot_table = role_demand.copy() plot_table.columns = [f"{r}\n(n={role_counts[r]:,})" for r in ROLES] fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 7.5)) annotated_heatmap(ax, plot_table, SEQUENTIAL, vmin=0, vmax=85, fmt=lambda v: f"{v:.0f}%", dark_from=40) ax.tick_params(axis="x", labelsize=9) ax.set_title("Skill Demand by Role Family (% of postings)", pad=34) save_figure("skill_demand_by_role.png") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Share of postings in each role family that request each skill. Skills are ordered by overall demand.](skill_gap_analysis_files/figure-html/fig-role-demand-output-1.png){#fig-role-demand width=861 height=711} ::: ::: - **SQL is the one skill every role needs.** It appears in 36% of Business Analyst postings and 80% of Business Intelligence postings. - **Business Intelligence roles are tool-heavy:** Tableau (63%), Power BI (52%), and Python (48%) follow SQL. - **Business Analyst roles are the most business-focused:** business requirements (39%), business analysis (34%), and Excel (29%) sit alongside SQL, while Python appears in only 14%. - **Data Scientist roles** are led by Python (82%) and machine learning (45%), and **Data Engineer roles** by Python, SQL, and data pipelines. ## 3. Career Evaluation Logic: Team Skills Against Market Requirements Job postings list skills but not the proficiency level employers expect. To compare the two, we set a **target level** for each skill using a transparent rule based on how often the skill is requested across all postings: | Demand in postings | Target level | |---|:---:| | 20% or more of postings | 4 (Advanced) | | 10% to 19.9% | 3 (Intermediate) | | Under 10% | 2 (Basic knowledge) | For each member and skill: - **Gap** = target level − current rating (0 if the member already meets the target) - **Priority score** = average team gap × share of postings The priority score favors skills that are both widely requested *and* weak across the team. The Improvement Plan in Section 4 uses the same rule. ::: {#build-gaps .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} def target_level(share): if share >= 20: return 4 if share >= 10: return 3 return 2 share = demand["Share of postings (%)"] targets = share.map(target_level) member_gaps = (targets - df_skills[targets.index]).clip(lower=0) # members x skills gap_table = pd.DataFrame( { "Demand (%)": share, "Target level": targets, "Team average": df_skills[targets.index].mean().round(2), } ) gap_table = gap_table.join(member_gaps.T.add_suffix(" gap")) gap_table["Average gap"] = member_gaps.mean().round(2) gap_table["Priority score"] = (gap_table["Average gap"] * share / 100).round(2) gap_table = gap_table.sort_values(["Priority score", "Demand (%)"], ascending=False) # Saved as a handoff for the Improvement Plan and Career Strategy pages gap_table.to_csv("data/processed/skill_gap_table.csv", index_label="Skill") ``` ::: ### Where the Team Falls Short ::: {#cell-fig-gap-comparison .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} plot_df = gap_table.iloc[::-1] y = np.arange(len(plot_df)) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 7.5)) short = plot_df["Team average"] < plot_df["Target level"] line_colors = [LIGHT_BLUE if s else "#DDE3E5" for s in short] ax.hlines(y, plot_df["Team average"], plot_df["Target level"], color=line_colors, linewidth=3) ax.scatter(plot_df["Target level"], y, s=90, facecolor="white", edgecolor=NAVY, linewidth=2, zorder=3, label="Target level") ax.scatter(plot_df["Team average"], y, s=80, color=TEAL, edgecolor="white", linewidth=1.5, zorder=4, label="Team average") ax.set_yticks(y, plot_df.index) ax.set_xticks(range(1, 6), ["1\nBeginner", "2\nBasic", "3\nIntermediate", "4\nAdvanced", "5\nExpert"]) ax.set_xlim(0.7, 5.3) ax.grid(axis="x", color=GRID, linewidth=0.8) ax.set_axisbelow(True) ax.spines[["top", "right", "left"]].set_visible(False) ax.tick_params(axis="y", length=0) ax.legend(loc="lower right", frameon=False) ax.set_title("Team Average vs. Target Level (highest priority at top)") save_figure("skill_gap_comparison.png") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Team average (filled dot) against the target level (open ring). Blue lines show the distance to close; gray lines show where the team already exceeds the target. Skills are ordered by priority score.](skill_gap_analysis_files/figure-html/fig-gap-comparison-output-1.png){#fig-gap-comparison width=765 height=710} ::: ::: ### Individual Gaps ::: {#cell-fig-member-gaps .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} g = member_gaps.T.loc[gap_table.index] fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6.5, 7.5)) annotated_heatmap(ax, g, GAP_SCALE, vmin=0, vmax=3, fmt=lambda v: f"+{v:.0f}", dark_from=3, blank_zero=True) ax.grid(which="minor", color=GRID, linewidth=1) ax.set_title("Levels Needed to Reach Target (priority order)", pad=28) save_figure("member_skill_gaps.png") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Levels each member needs to gain to reach the target. Blank cells mean the target is already met.](skill_gap_analysis_files/figure-html/fig-member-gaps-output-1.png){#fig-member-gaps width=633 height=711} ::: ::: ### Gaps Measured Against Each Member's Target Role The targets above use demand across all postings. Because demand differs so much by role, we repeat the comparison using the postings for each member's own target role, applying the same target rule to that role's demand. ::: {#tbl-role-gaps .cell tbl-cap='Each member\'s skills that fall short of the target for their own role, ordered by demand in that role.' execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} TARGET_ROLES = { "Jenna": ["Business Intelligence", "Business Analyst"], "Mariam": ["Business Analyst"], "Juan": ["Data Scientist"], } rows = [] for member, roles in TARGET_ROLES.items(): role_skills = panel.loc[panel["role_family"].isin(roles), "skills"] for skill, name in ratings["panel_skill_name"].items(): role_share = role_skills.map(lambda s, name=name: name in s).mean() * 100 target = target_level(role_share) current = int(ratings.loc[skill, member]) if target > current: rows.append( { "Member": member, "Target role": " / ".join(roles), "Skill": skill, "Demand in role (%)": round(role_share, 1), "Current": current, "Target": target, "Gap": target - current, } ) role_gaps = pd.DataFrame(rows) role_gaps["Member"] = pd.Categorical(role_gaps["Member"], MEMBERS, ordered=True) role_gaps = role_gaps.sort_values(["Member", "Demand in role (%)"], ascending=[True, False]) role_gaps.style.hide(axis="index").format(precision=1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=11} ```{=html}

Business requirements (Intermediate to Advanced) and Python follow. Her BI tool skills already meet the target for these roles. - **Mariam (Business Analyst):** SQL is the clear first priority, followed by business analysis and Excel, which each appear in about a third of Business Analyst postings. Python appears in only 14% of these postings, so it matters less for her target role than the market-wide view suggests. - **Juan (Data Scientist):** Python and machine learning are both requested in most Data Scientist postings, so machine learning is more urgent for him than the market-wide view suggests. ### Gap Summary Table ::: {#tbl-gap-summary .cell tbl-cap='Skill gaps by member across all postings, ordered by priority score.' execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} gap_table.rename_axis("Skill").reset_index().style.hide(axis="index").format(precision=2).format("{:.1f}", subset=["Demand (%)"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=12} ```{=html}

Closing them matters for every target role on the team. 2. **Data pipelines are the largest gap relative to demand.** They appear in about a fifth of all postings (and nearly half of Data Engineer postings), and the whole team is at Beginner or Basic level. 3. **The team's business skills already meet the market.** Across all postings, business requirements, business analysis, data analysis, Excel, and communication meet their targets for all three members. These are genuine strengths for the business analyst and BI roles that Jenna and Mariam are targeting. 4. **The team is complementary.** Juan's BI tool expertise, Jenna's Excel, analysis, and communication skills, and Mariam's business requirements skills cover different parts of the market, so peer teaching inside the team is a realistic first step before outside courses. 5. **Mariam has the most ground to cover, Juan the least.** Mariam's gaps span SQL, Python, and the BI tools, while Juan's remaining gaps are concentrated in Python, SQL, pipelines, and machine learning. ### Limitations - **Assumed targets:** Postings do not state a proficiency level. The target-level rule is a team assumption, stated above so readers can adjust it. - **Self-ratings:** Team ratings are self-assessed and not independently tested. Some ratings were carried over from an earlier skill list and mapped to the closest v2 skill, as recorded in `team_skills_v2.csv`. - **Required versus preferred:** Postings do not separate required skills from preferred ones, so demand shares may overstate how essential a skill is. - **Small role groups:** Business Intelligence has only 81 postings, so its role-specific shares are less precise than those for the larger role families. ## 4. Improvement Plan ::: {#plan-setup .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} import json import pandas as pd _MEMBERS = ["Jenna", "Mariam", "Juan"] _panel = pd.read_csv("data/processed/career_market_panel.csv") _n = len(_panel) _posting_skills = _panel["SKILLS_NAME"].fillna("[]").map( lambda s: set(json.loads(s)) if s.startswith("[") else set() ) plan = pd.read_csv("data/processed/team_skills_v2.csv").set_index("skill") plan["Demand (%)"] = plan["panel_skill_name"].map( lambda name: round(_posting_skills.map(lambda x: name in x).sum() / _n * 100, 1) ) def _target_level(share): if share >= 20: return 4 if share >= 10: return 3 return 2 plan["Target"] = plan["Demand (%)"].map(_target_level) _rows = [] for _member in _MEMBERS: for _skill, _row in plan.iterrows(): _rating = _row[_member] if pd.isna(_rating): continue _gap = max(_row["Target"] - _rating, 0) if _gap > 0: _rows.append( { "Member": _member, "Skill": _skill, "Current": int(_rating), "Target": int(_row["Target"]), "Gap": int(_gap), "Demand (%)": _row["Demand (%)"], "Priority": round(_gap * _row["Demand (%)"] / 100, 2), } ) plan_gaps = pd.DataFrame(_rows) _pending = {m: [s for s in plan.index if pd.isna(plan.loc[s, m])] for m in _MEMBERS} _pending = {m: s for m, s in _pending.items() if s} if _pending: pending_note = ( "Some ratings are still pending: " + "; ".join(f"{m} for {', '.join(s)}" for m, s in _pending.items()) + ". Those skills are left out of the member's priorities until they are rated." ) else: pending_note = "All three members have rated every skill on the list." ``` ::: This section turns the skill gaps into a plan. For each team member we identify the skills to work on first, suggest courses, certifications, and projects that close those gaps, and describe how the team can use its complementary strengths. ### 4.1 Setting Priorities We use the same rule as Section 3 to set a target level for each skill, based on how often it is requested in the postings. A skill in 20 percent or more of postings gets a target of 4 (Advanced), one in 10 to 19.9 percent a target of 3 (Intermediate), and anything less a target of 2 (Basic knowledge). With the v2 data every skill on the list is measured directly in the postings, so no targets are assumed. A member's gap is the target minus their current rating, or zero if they already meet it. Their priority for a skill is that gap weighted by the skill's share of postings, which favors skills that are both in demand and far from the member's current level. ::: {#tbl-plan-targets .cell tbl-cap='Target level for each skill, set by its share of postings.' execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} plan[["Demand (%)", "Target"] + _MEMBERS].sort_values("Demand (%)", ascending=False).rename_axis("Skill").reset_index().style.hide(axis="index").format("{:.1f}", subset=["Demand (%)"]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=15} ```{=html}

Python, SQL, and data pipelines are both the most requested skills in the postings and the team's largest gaps, so the plan below is built around studying them together rather than as three separate plans. ### 4.3 Courses, Certifications, and Projects Each project uses this site's own data, so practice time also improves the project. | Skill | Free learning | Certification | Practice project | |---|---|---|---| | Python | Kaggle Learn: Python and Pandas | Not needed at this stage | Recreate the Market Baseline charts from the panel in pandas | | SQL | Kaggle Learn: Intro to SQL and Advanced SQL | Not needed at this stage | Rewrite the panel's filtering steps as Spark SQL queries | | Data Pipelines | Data Engineering Zoomcamp by DataTalks.Club, self-paced | Databricks Certified Data Engineer Associate, later stage | Turn `build_panel.py` into a scheduled pipeline that refreshes the panel | | Databricks | Databricks Academy self-paced courses | Databricks Certified Data Engineer Associate (about \$200) | Run the panel build in a Databricks notebook | | Machine Learning | Kaggle Learn: Intro to Machine Learning; Where the strongest member still has a gap themselves, as with Python and SQL, the team studies together rather than relying on one person to teach. In practice: - **A weekly study session** of about an hour, working through the same Kaggle Learn or Zoomcamp module and comparing solutions. - **Rotating who writes the code.** For each remaining module of this project, the member with the largest gap writes the first version of the code, and the strongest member reviews it through a pull request. The work gets done and the practice counts double. - **Pairing on the BI tools.** The members strongest in Power BI and Tableau walk the others through rebuilding one Market Baseline chart in each tool. - **Business framing from the business-side members.** Members targeting business analyst roles lead on turning findings into requirements and recommendations for the Career Strategy page. ### 4.5 Timeline | Weeks | Focus | Who | |---|---|---| | 1 to 4 | Python and SQL foundations through Kaggle Learn, with the weekly study session | Everyone | | 5 to 8 | Data pipelines through the Data Engineering Zoomcamp; Power BI and Tableau practice for members with gaps there | Everyone, plus individual BI practice | | 9 to 12 | Machine learning basics and the salary-prediction project, which feeds the Predictive Modeling page | Everyone | | After week 12 | One certification each, matched to target role: PL-300 or Tableau Data Analyst for business intelligence and business analyst roles, Databricks Data Engineer Associate for data roles | Individual | A member's target role can matter as much as the posting counts.
